title: Minimise Tree Diameter by Removing Leaves
statement:
You are given an undirected tree with `n` nodes numbered `0` to `n - 1`, and an integer `k`.

In one operation you may remove a **leaf**: a node that currently has exactly one neighbour in the tree. Removing a node also removes its single edge. You may perform **at most `k` operations**, choosing the leaves in any order; after each removal the tree is the remaining connected tree. A tree with a single node has no neighbours, so that last node is never a leaf and cannot be removed.

The **diameter** of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path between any two of its nodes (a single node has diameter `0`).

Return the **smallest diameter** you can obtain after performing at most `k` leaf removals.
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `n` and `k`.
Each of the next `n - 1` lines contains two integers `u` and `v`, describing an edge between nodes `u` and `v` (0-indexed).
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum possible diameter (number of edges).
constraints: The edges form a valid tree

examples.explanation: The tree is a path of 6 nodes with diameter 5. Removing leaf 0 and then leaf 5 leaves the path 1-2-3-4 with diameter 3.

This is a complete binary tree of 7 nodes (diameter 4). Remove leaves 3 and 4; node 1 then becomes a leaf, so remove it too. What remains is node 2 joined to nodes 0, 5 and 6, a star with diameter 2. One fewer operation would leave a diameter of at least 3.
With enough operations you can remove leaves 1, 2, 3 and 4 one by one, leaving only node 0, whose diameter is 0. The last node can never be removed, so extra operations are unused.

hints: Removing leaves one at a time always leaves a connected piece of the tree, and every connected piece of size at least n - k can be reached this way. So you are looking for the connected sub-tree with at least n - k nodes that has the smallest diameter.

A sub-tree with diameter D fits inside a ball around its centre: a vertex and radius D/2 when D is even, or an edge and radius (D-1)/2 when D is odd. Counting the nodes in such a ball tells you how large a sub-tree of that diameter can be.

For every vertex and every edge as a centre, run a BFS (a multi-source BFS from both ends for an edge) and find the smallest radius whose ball contains at least n - k nodes. The best centre gives the answer; an O(n^2) total is fine.
